Supporting unpaid carers to remain in work (Department for Work and Pensions)

Background

In 2017, DWP’s Human-Centred Design Science (or DWP Behavioural Science as it was then called) and carers employment policy teams sought to understand why unpaid carers leave employment and whether there was more government could do to prevent this.

Recognising this challenge cuts across the remit of multiple departments in central government, we invited colleagues from the Departments of Health (as it was then), Business, Government Equalities Office and Treasury to a workshop to map respective departmental objectives around unpaid carers to explore any tensions or trade-offs. We then used detailed, evidence-based personas to consider citizen experiences and support needs from the point that care needs first emerge onwards. Collectively, we mapped the journeys that each persona ‘should’ take in light of the then landscape of policies, services and entitlements (in other words – the ‘ideal’ journey at that time). We then considered the journey that each persona would be likely to take in reality, bearing in mind the range of barriers they faced, including a lack of time, a lack of energy, and limited knowledge of what can feel like a confusing and fragmented system of services and support.

This exercise highlighted that families might well have significant unmet needs during the earliest days and weeks after care needs emerge, when many highly consequential decisions are being made, often under great pressure and without much support. This led to a hypothesis: Under-informed decision-making early in people’s caring journeys contributes to people feeling forced to leave work to care later on.

Problem definition: exploring our hypothesis

A cross-departmental, jointly funded ‘discovery project’ was established to test and explore our hypothesis. We built a community of around45 experts and organisations across government, charities, academia and the private sector, as well as unpaid carers themselves, and co-designed research with working people at different stages of caring. Not only was it vital to gain multiple perspectives on this complex and emotive challenge, but we also recognised the vast range of information touchpoints that influence care choices, and that many of these were not owned by Government.

Throughout this collaboration we regularly shared, tested and iterated our developing understanding of caring experiences and the systems they navigate. We shared information verbally and in writing, but also – crucially – through diagrams and visuals. These visuals (Figures 17-21) helped to make complex concepts clear, overcome differences in the way people and organisations used language, and focused our conversations and thinking.

Research with carers

Qualitative research conducted for us by Ipsos MORI revealed a ‘default journey’ with carers reporting feeling that they had no option but to take on unpaid care. People experienced pressure to make early decisions hastily without understanding how care needs might evolve, or considering the possible long-term consequences for their wellbeing, relationships, finances or employment. Early on, people didn’t see themselves as ‘carers’ or seek information or support. When carers did access information and support, it was often only after a point of crisis when the opportunity to remain in work had already passed.

Figure 17. The ‘default’ caring journey.

Identification of need

Initiation of care

Managing

Stress

Crisis

Receiving support

Linking individual decisions to societal impacts

We produced a causal sequence and impact map (Figure 18) illustrating how the default journey connected to key societal-level impacts that organisations in our community valued, enabling collective scrutiny and challenge.

Figure 18. Default caring journey impact sequence map.

Defining informed decision-making for our target users

We collaboratively developed a detailed set of information needs for a previously under-recognised and un-named group: ‘potential carers’ (i.e. working people facing decisions about work and care). The distinction between ‘potential carers’ and ‘carers’ highlighted the gap in thinking across organisations in the system.

Stakeholders began to see and talk about the problem differently. Most information and policy had been designed for established ‘carers’, but this didn’t always meet the distinct needs of those making pivotal early decisions which could close off opportunities for remaining in work later on. Our ‘informed decision model’ (Figure 19) mapped groups of information needs. The model contrasted starkly with the above ‘default journey’.

Figure 19. The informed decision model for choices about work and care

At each step in the model, potential carers have related information needs. For example:

As a potential carer, to make an informed decision I need…

to consider my own needs as well as those of others, and information that doesn’t cause feelings of guilt I might experience around doing this

accurate, up-to-date information that reflects my current options (bearing in mind the system of support and services changes frequently at both the national and local level)

accurate, up-to-date information about my family member’s care needs now, and what caring activities will need to be performed to meet those needs

information and practical advice about how to negotiate with others and to advocate for myself and the person with care needs.

Mapping the information landscape

We also mapped the system of information and advice relevant to unpaid carers from the citizen’s perspective. Taking a systems-wide view highlighted an enormous sense-making burden on potential carers. Informed decision-making required seeking out and navigating a vast and complex range of information often not designed with their needs in mind, which they may not know exists, and which was in effect invisible to many who didn’t see themselves as ‘carers’.

In the centre of the system map (Figure 20) is the working potential carer. Types of information source are colour coded, and bold links represent sources that a working person is most likely to be in contact with early on with their journey. Dotted lines represent connections between sources which a potential carer may or may never find without additional help or luck.

Figure 20. A working person’s care information landscape.

Detailing Barriers

A fuller set of barriers to addressing the information needs was also detailed using an adapted version of the Individual Social Material (ISM) model of behaviour. The schematic below (Figure 21) shows five categories of barrier: individual, interpersonal, social, cultural and informational. This helped to clarify that a digital or communications intervention was only likely to be able to affect information-level barriers but should take the other barriers to decision-making into account.

Figure 21. Barriers to informed decision-making about paid work and care

Progress against the systemic problem

We led workshops with our community and carers to think creatively about how barriers within the information landscape might be removed to better meet needs and enable more informed decision-making. Given the complexity of the problem, we were looking for ways to make progress, rather than trying to achieve a complete solution. Convening the community was itself a catalyst for new partnerships, facilitating join up on local improvements.

During a hiatus due to the Covid pandemic we used our insights to help the NHS design a leaflet for those being discharged from NHS hospitals, their families and loved ones.[footnote 27] Afterwards, the next stage of work continued with a similarly open and collaborative ethos. In early 2022, partnering with the UK Government’s Policy Lab and University of the Arts London (UAL), we re-convened some of our community of experts and carers to help identify and prototype potential solutions. Through a series of co-design workshops, we explored and developed:

How information products can reach and convey options to potential carers most effectively at the earliest practical points

How potential carers might best be supported to make sense of their situation, options and considerations involved in care choices

What conversation support might aid sensitive and collaborative discussions between potential carers, employers, healthcare professionals, family and those with care needs

How potential carers might be supported in navigating a range of online information

How different information touchpoints might proactively serve information to potential carers at an early stage

What kinds of language and terms are and are not effective in communicating with potential carers

How carers might be supported to give their own needs due weight in decision-making

How organisations might collaborate through a ‘community of practice’ to make progress towards system-wide improvements.

In December 2022 DWP funded a multidisciplinary team of policy professionals, digital practitioners, analysts, and behavioural and design scientists to refine these ideas, bringing them into sharper relief and exploration with potential carers. This led to improving ways that existing pages on GOV.UK could be better signposted to, and launching new web pages on the government’s Job Help campaign site for people working and supporting someone’s health or care[footnote 28].

Enabling more informed decision-making about work and care cannot be achieved through isolated information products, however, or without ongoing extensive collaboration between the organisations in the information landscape. Continued, iterative co-design across the system will be vital to making progress against the problem.

Systemic approaches to improving resettlement from custody to the community (Ministry of Justice)

Context

In 2021, almost 80 percent of crime was committed by someone who had offended previously. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has estimated that reoffending costs society approximately £22.7 billion a year.

With that in mind, in late 2022, the Ministry of Justice wanted to establish a vision for how we improve resettlement from custody. The aims would be to both reduce reoffending by ensuring effective resettlement back into the community, and to protect the public. We needed to be comprehensive and reflect the complex underlying causes that lead to reoffending but also ensure what we developed was understandable and deliverable.

This project brought together three service designers and three policy makers to analyse the current state of the prison resettlement system and identify the best approach to improve provision. Our goal was to establish an understanding of what an effective system would look like that was both ambitious and outcome focused, but achievable within political and organisational constraints (e.g. budget, team skills and setup).

The vision would need to take into account the perspectives of people in prison and on probation, frontline staff and managers across the prison and probation system, and charities and other groups who work with people in prison and on probation. It would need to be informed by existing government policy and operational realities. This information would provide an accurate representation of the as-is state of the criminal justice system and provide a to-be vision for resettlement that is desirable, feasible, and viable.

Building our knowledge of the whole system

Our multidisciplinary team members built their knowledge of the system by engaging with over 500 people across the justice system, including colleagues from the Ministry of Justice, His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS), voluntary and community services, as well as people with lived experience of the criminal justice system. The three designers on the team were drawing on their experience over two years working on the innovative ‘Prison Leavers Project’[footnote 29], during which they worked with colleagues in and around the justice system to explore the causes of reoffending through four explorations, three pilot projects, and 10 workstreams. That work included interviews, workshops, and other research activities with over 400 people experiencing or working in the justice system.

Policy colleagues built their knowledge by conducting policy sprints, breaking the journey through prison into four stages — entering prison, in prison, preparing for release, and post-release — and conducted round-tables and direct interviews with more than 100 people engaged in those processes.

All this gave us a clear understanding of the main challenges across the resettlement journey from induction in prison to post-release, when people have resettled back in the community.

Synthesising that knowledge into a clear and comprehensive vision

The research findings were analysed using a system-thinking approach based on an ‘iceberg’ framework, to help us understand and then describe how the system functions and behaves. The iceberg framework starts with the ‘events’ that we can all see happening in a system, and how they come together as a recurring ‘pattern’ of events. Going deeper, we explored the many and varied ‘structural elements’ of the system that lead to this outcome, as well as the underlying beliefs and attitudes held about and within the system that influence those within it.

The think tank New Philanthropy Capital (NPC) provides a very clear and useful summary of the iceberg framework[footnote 30] (Figure 22) and how they used it to begin their analysis of the criminal justice sector.

Figure 22. Iceberg systems thinking model

Our team mapped these events, patterns, structural elements, and mental models across the resettlement system, as we understood them, zooming into the finer details and then zooming out to describe the interactions between them. From this combination of boxes, arrows, and eventually, summary narratives, a comprehensive system map emerged, showcasing the complexity of the system and the interconnectedness of all its parts.

While the team all came into this work with a deep understanding of the core factors driving reoffending, synthesising data in this way was a new approach. The system map helped us distinguish levers for long-term change from the more indirect approaches that were less likely to address root causes of problems.

It was challenging to analyse the large amount of interrelated information we had gathered. We approached this challenge by using the ‘five whys’[footnote 31] (sometimes the six, seven, eight whys!). This technique helped deepen our understanding of the complex issues. We used our visual design skills to demonstrate how all the issues identified were inter-related, and then translated this into clear, compelling written narratives that could easily be understood and used by policy and operational teams to drive change across the opportunity areas identified.

This combination of logical analysis, visual mapping, and narrative development enabled us to understand and describe a system in ways that acknowledged its incredible complexity while being simple and clear enough to inform conversations on how to improve the system moving forward.

Using the map to drive long-term change

After mapping the system, we resisted the urge to identify problems, list solutions and hand those over to operational partners to deliver. Instead, we identified ‘opportunity areas’ which could be targeted for further exploration, shared these with operational partners, and invited them to challenge the thinking, add their feedback, and discuss how the opportunity areas related to their delivery priorities. We then made the case for long-term exploration of system improvements across the range of areas, acknowledging the benefits of an iterative, design-led approach to learning and continuous improvement.

As a result of taking a design-led approach to this problem, we have been able to develop a deeper understanding of barriers to effective resettlement provision to inform policymaking and decisions moving forward. This understanding has been derived from the synthesised collective intelligence of hundreds of people living and breathing the justice system every day — on both sides of the bars.

Most fundamentally, this project has brought service-design methodologies to the heart of the organisation’s long-term strategy-setting and policymaking processes for the first time ever. In this way, the greatest impact of the work might be how it enables future service design work to take place within a major government department that traditionally only applied service design thinking to Digital aspects of its work.

Reflecting on the work, a policy advisor on the multidisciplinary team said:

“Working with service designers on this project has been invaluable. Their skill set has ensured that at every point, the impact on the person in prison was at the forefront of what we were trying to understand. Their systems thinking has enabled us to visualise the complexity of the resettlement system and reminded us how interlinked we are as an organisation.”

“The designers encouraged us to view any changes to the system as opportunities for iterative improvements, rather than the silver bullet solution we can sometimes search for.”

As the results of this project will continue to be seen in the months and years to come, the demand for service design will continue to grow throughout the organisation. This shift in mindset and change in approach will ultimately result in much better outcomes for people in prison and on probation, a safer public, and better value for money to the taxpayers.

If this approach leads to more effective and joined-up resettlement activities across the justice system and wider society — and therefore improves the outcomes for people leaving prison — not only will society be safer for all of us and ensure people leave prison with the right support, but the taxpayer could see improved value for money year on year.

This case study is also published on the Service Design Network website[footnote 32].

Understanding and communicating the lived experiences of disabled people (Policy Lab and Disability Unit)

Policy Lab took a design-led approach, deploying methods such as film ethnography and speculative design, to explore the lived experiences of disabled people.

In March 2019, a newly formed Disability Unit within the UK Government was tasked with starting a programme of ‘lived experience research’ to ensure disabled people’s lived experience shaped future policy development. While incomplete, the pre-existing evidence base clearly showed that disabled people experience worse outcomes in all areas of life compared to non-disabled people.

The Policy Lab – with its combination of design and research skills – partnered with Disability Unit to understand the daily experiences of disabled people. From June to October 2019, Policy Lab recruited and worked with 12 disabled people in England, developing film research material to understand their lives. Researchers used a range of methods, including in-depth interviews, ethnographically led film work, journey mapping, and diary writing. Policy Lab spent around 70 hours engaged in deep listening, observation and participation.

In March 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, we were re-commissioned to work again with original participants. Policy Lab researchers used remote video diaries and incorporated a speculative design exercise into the research to build evidence about people’s experiences of the pandemic.

Policy Lab was commissioned to create a picture of daily experiences of life in the UK with a disability. Disability Unit’s stated aim for the work was to “identify problems that could be resolved through policy change”[footnote 33]. The work illustrated the policy team’s desire to inform policy intent using design methodologies which capture lived experiences.

The ethnography explored a wide diversity of disabled experiences and presented specific examples in rich detail. The commissioner explained that the research “helps people stretch outside of their understanding” and reveals “how experiences might be very different from the assumptions that policymakers have.”

At the conclusion of the second stage of the research, participants were invited to explore an ideal future scenario in which some of their hopes and expectations from the COVID-19 pandemic had been realised through government policy. Participants were asked to describe what ‘better’ would look like for them, for experiences such as interacting with healthcare services. The contents of these conversations were designed into storyboards so that Disability Unit could more easily and directly engage policymakers in conversations about future policy. An example storyboard is shown in Figure 23. In this example. the participant imagined a near future where hygiene and other COVID-19 rules and policy were clearly stated across public spaces. Sanitation facilities would be widely available. People would be more understanding and considerate towards those who were clinically vulnerable, including wearing masks and giving space on pavements. Such action and disability awareness would become common place in education.

Figure 23. Example storyboard of ideal future.

Disability Unit used this emerging research to help set the direction for policymaking and evidence on disability-related issues. The Head of Evidence described, “we wanted to have a direction – a focus on daily lives and impact on daily lives, the glue in between the different bits of policy and a need to see the range of activities. That is what we got from it.”

As well as setting strategic direction, the ethnographic films were also used as part of further research via a survey to elicit further views from disabled people about their experiences. The films were published on social media alongside the survey.

Additionally, insights and quotes from the research were used by the Office for National Statistics to bring to life their statistical data releases[footnote 34]. The research was published in full by Disability Unit [footnote 35],[footnote 36].

The research outputs provided an engaging evidence base for Disability Unit to influence policy and strategy development across government. The commissioner reflected that the research “over time sharpened our own brand of Disability Unit. When we were talking to DfE, DWP and others, we had an edge to the conversation showing how these conversations relate to people.”

The films were also seen by the DWP Secretary of State at the time, “who was moved by what she was viewing” (DWP commissioner). The commissioner said: “to have that dialogue is just incredibly important and really valuable because from the very top it helps to shape what the government thinks about disability.” The films were also shown to all new starters in Disability Unit to ensure that people have an “initial understanding of what we’re doing and why we’re doing it”. The films are “a really good motivator to remind us why we are actually doing this.”

The ethnographic research was conducted over multiple years, making this a longitudinal study into people’s daily lives which fed insights on an ongoing basis into cross-government policy design.

Universal Credit service (Department for Work and Pensions)

Background

In 2013 the government introduced the most fundamental reforms to the welfare system for more than 60 years. This brought together six separate benefits previously administered by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), HMRC and local authorities into one combined benefit administered by DWP: Universal Credit.

This fundamental welfare reform aims to reward work, encourage responsibility, make work pay, support aspiration and help those who need it most.

Universal Credit provides a means-tested, dynamic, monthly payment that claimants are entitled to based on their circumstances in each monthly assessment period. Case managers support the management of claims, and work coaches support people with job searching or to increase their earnings.

The service is operating at scale across the UK: 7.3 million people were claiming Universal Credit in November 2024. It’s a benefit for people who are unemployed, in work on low income, or unable to work because of a health condition, disability or caring responsibilities. A claim can last throughout the working-age life of the person claiming until state retirement age.

The Universal Credit service team view ‘the service’ as the totality of the offer that supports the needs of claimants. This case study focuses specifically on the approach to designing the service and its associated operations and support offers across multiple channels: online, telephone and jobcentres.

Holistic service design to meet user needs and lower barriers to the service

Universal Credit claimants can self-serve to make their claim and can view or provide up-to-date information at any time. There is a range of operational responsibilities and teams (DWP staff) who interact with claims and support claimants through multiple service channels.

The service experience is built and delivered digitally and augmented with interactions between agents and claimants over the telephone and in jobcentres. Additional support is provided by home visits or ‘Help to claim’ through Citizens Advice.

It is designed by in-house multidisciplinary teams. New features and iterations to the service are delivered every week.

Design hypotheses describe concepts or prototypes that help teams ‘test and learn’ to understand requirements and user behaviours that might not have been known in initial scoping. Iterating user journeys to gather data and insight builds confidence that service outcomes are delivered as intended before scaling to more users.

Figure 24. Visual showing the Universal Credit design cycle.

As the service matures it provides more opportunities to learn and iterate. Knowledge gathered through interactions with wider services, infrastructure and users cannot easily be analysed unless observed in an ‘as live’ situation.

In January 2023 the team designing the journeys to move legacy benefit claimants to Universal Credit described their work as building an ‘earliest testable service’. The testing was designed to enable teams to learn from the experiences of people claiming with additional, dedicated agent support. For example, we discovered that many people would seek help to make a claim. As a result, it would take longer for them to respond to the request to move to Universal Credit, so the team experimented with sending reminders through different channels and varied their timing and frequency.

This was not a scalable pilot, but a baseline service used to learn about claimants’ needs effectively and safely, and to optimise for outcomes and scaling over time. It was the first step in the ‘discovery’ work[footnote 37].

The service response during COVID-19 pandemic

During COVID-19, the needs of claimants, and the environment around them, changed rapidly and dramatically. Many claimants had little or no prior experience of the welfare system. DWP and the Universal Credit service had to respond quickly at a time when its own operational and corporate resources were compromised. Face-to-face channels became unavailable, and the number of claims increased massively.

It was imperative that Universal Credit could continue to support and pay existing claimants while also meeting the immediate needs of this significant number of new claimants in these unexpected and challenging circumstances.

Having a service that was designed and built by an in-house, highly trained and by-now highly experienced multidisciplinary team meant we could quickly adapt to this rapidly changing environment. We could pivot to address the most pressing problems and deliver tactical and strategic solutions to support citizens in extraordinary circumstances. The service scaled to successfully handle a doubling of claims in just a few weeks.

It has been widely recognised that no other service would have been as robust and able to respond to this unprecedented challenge as effectively as Universal Credit did.

Figure 25. Graph showing people on Universal Credit, Great Britain, January 2019 to January 2024. Data taken from government Universal Credit statistics.

The benefits of a collaborative, iterative design approach

The Universal Credit service went live in November 2014. There was a conscious decision to build it incrementally. Carefully negotiating its policy and design complexity, and learning about user behaviour, meant that scaling occurred gradually and safely.

Although Universal Credit’s programme status is due to end in March 2025, the continuous design approach and team structure is likely to stay largely the same. This will help us to maintain the culture and ways of working that have supported effective design and delivery during the programme period. For example:

empowered multidisciplinary teams: digital, policy and operational teams working in partnership to optimise the design and delivery of an effective multi-channel holistic service

the supply and maintenance of the infrastructure required to keep this 24/7 service performant, secure and delivering agreed outcomes

appropriate and proportionate governance to empower those who are best placed to make evidence-based decisions

governance that supports the prioritisation of strategic goals, and teams empowered to propose which problems to focus on, to discover and deliver the best solutions

the use of roadmaps based on user needs, data and other evidence; and supported by ideation, prototyping, problem scoping and research driven by previously agreed service goals

the right balance between service stability, operational efficiency, effective user experience, supporting those with barriers and protecting the public purse

alignment with the departmental strategic direction.

The service will never be a ‘finished product’. Ways of working have developed to continuously iterate the service through collaborative design processes with decisions based on data and evidence.

The ‘landlord portal’ is an example of this. The business case for Universal Credit did not anticipate the full range of user needs of, and necessary interactions with, providers of social rented housing, such as housing associations.

Over time, the service team gathered evidence of problems, for example in the timely and accurate uprating of rental rates each year for many thousands of tenants claiming Universal Credit. From this they identified user needs and worked closely with social rental sector landlords to develop a solution. The landlords took part in user research and helped to test the various prototypes that were developed. And the team provided training and guidance to the landlords’ staff.

The solution was a supplementary online service that landlords can use directly to manage tenant and payments data. This has considerably improved the timeliness of Universal Credit housing payments and improved the relationship with the social rental sector.

Designed to deliver outcomes

The Universal Credit programme is funded to design and deliver the service with welfare reform outcomes. The 2018 business case was based not only on financial benefits but also on the goal of delivering broader societal impacts.

One example of that: single parents on Universal Credit are five percentage points more likely to have been in work within six months of making their claim compared to those on legacy benefits.

The business case also includes reducing the cost of administering benefits and automating tasks and calculations, where appropriate, to give agents space to focus on supporting claimants.

The annual cost of administering a Universal Credit claim was estimated to be £195 in April 2023 (across 5,085,900 cases) compared with £593 in April 2018 (505,400 cases). This was achieved this through system enhancements, more automation, and use of digital channels, enabling case managers to support a greater number of claimants.

Perhaps the most important outcome is this: in October 2023, 97 percent of households in receipt of Universal Credit received all of their payment on time. 99 percent received some or all of their payment on time. This figure has been largely consistent since April 2020.

Universal Credit is a service that replaces not one but six legacy benefits, and which dynamically adapts, month by month, to the individual circumstances of millions of people. It is the foundation for a transformed welfare state, one responsive to the needs of the people who rely on it.
